category: The core three: in, on, at

entries.complement: noun phrase; pronoun in the objective case (at him, at us, at whom); gerund (good at cooking, no good at explaining things); wh-clause (shocked at what it cost, good at what she does); a bare article-less noun in frozen idiom only (at work, at school, at home, at night, at war, at sea). Never a bare infinitive (good at to swim) and never a finite that-clause — surprised at that he left is impossible; write surprised that he left or surprised at the fact that he left. The gerund may carry its own subject (surprised at his leaving so early, annoyed at the neighbors parking there), and a wh-word is fine (at what point, at whatever price) while whether is not — it depends at whether is impossible, because that frame belongs to on. With the reaction adjectives the patterns divide cleanly: shocked at the price takes a noun phrase, shocked that the price had doubled takes the bare that-clause with no preposition at all, and shocked by is the passive-agent alternative. Unlike in and on, at has no adverb use at all: it always has an object, even a stranded one.
entries.pattern: at [noun phrase] · [verb] at [noun phrase] · [adjective] at [noun phrase or verb-ing] · [noun] at [noun phrase] (a look at the numbers) · stranded: What are you looking at? — the motel we stayed at · pied-piped (formal): At which point did you notice?
entries.contrast: The point member of the in / on / at system. Against in: arrive at a building or event but arrive in a city or country; at school is where you are standing, in school is enrolled; at the store is the errand, in the store is the interior. Against on: at the corner is a meeting point, on the corner is a building's address, in the corner is the inside angle of a room. Against to: throw it at him means he is the target and may get hit, throw it to him is a pass; shout at is anger, shout to is distance. Against by in the spatial sense: at the door is the point you are stationed at and implies purpose, while by the door only says beside, with no claim about what you are doing there. On the calendar at takes the smallest unit of the three: at 6:15 is a tick, on Tuesday a day, in March a container.
entries.meaning: The preposition of the point. Whatever it governs is treated as dimensionless — a dot on a map, a tick on a clock, a value on a scale — which generates its spatial, temporal, target and rate senses alike. It never treats its object as a space with an interior; the moment a location has an inside worth mentioning, English switches to in. Senses: 1. A point in space (at the bus stop, at the second light), including the at the top / bottom / front / back / end of frame that picks one point out of a larger object. 2. A place named by what happens there — institutions, workplaces, events (at work, at a wedding). 3. Engaged in an activity — the article-less at work, at play, at prayer, at study, at lunch, at table, plus bare at it, where the phrase names an occupation rather than a place. 4. Where someone can be reached — phone numbers, extensions, email addresses, handles (at 555-0143); the @ sign is read aloud as at, but the symbol is the old commercial at of sense 12 and meant at the rate of for centuries before it meant at this domain. 5. A clock time or exact moment (at 6:15, at midnight). 6. An age or a stage (at nineteen, at that point in the season). 7. A target, often hostile and possibly missed (stare at, throw a rock at). 8. An attempt — a try, a shot, a stab, a crack or a go at something, plus guess at, work at, pick at, hint at, grasp at; like the target sense it leaves open whether the aim succeeded. 9. The stimulus behind a reaction (shocked at, annoyed at). 10. Prompted by, or on a given signal (at the mayor's request, at the first sign of smoke, at gunpoint, at your convenience). 11. Skill or ability (good at, hopeless at). 12. Rate, price, speed or level (at four dollars a gallon, at 350) — the commercial sense the @ sign stands for. 13. Distance, range or remove (at close range, at arm's length, at thirty thousand feet). 14. A state or condition, in a closed set of article-less idioms (at war, at rest, at risk, at fault, at large, at a loss, at ease). 15. Fixed adverbial phrases of degree and manner (at least, at most, at best, at once, at last, at random, at all — the last only in negatives, questions and conditionals), plus the at its + superlative frame. Stranding: at strands freely (What are you looking at?, the motel we stayed at), cannot be pied-piped after that or a zero relative, and because it has no adverb use it can never be left pointing at nothing — Where are you at? doubles the location where already supplies.
examples: She's waiting at the bus stop on Fourth.
Turn left at the second light.
He's at work until six.
We met at a wedding in Tulsa.
The two of them were at it again by Thursday.
She's been at work on the same chapter since April.
You can reach me at 555-0143.
Questions go to the help desk at support@example.com.
The flight boards at 6:15.
At midnight the fireworks started.
She published her first novel at nineteen.
At that point in the season, nobody expected a comeback.
Stop staring at me.
Some kid threw a rock at the window.
Take a crack at the first two problems and skip the rest.
Don't guess at the dosage — call the pharmacy.
I was shocked at how much the repair cost.
She was annoyed at being left off the list.
The hearing was rescheduled at the mayor's request.
At the first sign of smoke, the whole floor emptied.
He's hopeless at directions.
She's gotten very good at saying no.
Gas is at four dollars a gallon this week.
Bake it at 350 for forty minutes.
The photo was taken at close range.
She keeps everybody at arm's length.
The two countries have been at war since spring.
Half the neighborhood is at risk of flooding.
At least twenty people showed up.
I didn't like the ending at all.

entries.complement: noun phrase; pronoun in the objective case (in it, in them); gerund (interested in going, succeeded in getting the permit); wh-clause (a difference in what they charge, no say in who gets hired); a bare noun or adjective in frozen idiom only (in short, in general, in full, in private, in public). Never a bare infinitive (interested in to go) and never a finite that-clause. The sequence in that + clause (It's unusual in that it has no engine) is a fixed two-word subordinator meaning insofar as — a conjunction, not this preposition taking a clause.
entries.pattern: in [noun phrase] · in [verb-ing] · [verb] in [noun phrase] · [noun] in [noun phrase] (a change in policy) · [adjective] in [noun phrase] (rich in iron) · stranded: the town I grew up in — This bed has been slept in · pied-piped (formal): the town in which I grew up
entries.contrast: The container member of the in / on / at system. Against at: in the store is inside the building, at the store is the errand; in school is enrolled, at school is present. Against on: enclosure versus surface — in the car but on the bus; in bed but on the bed. Against into: in is position and into is the crossing of the boundary — He was in the pool is not He jumped into the pool — though after ordinary motion verbs American English uses plain in freely (jump in the pool, put it in the drawer); use into when the crossing itself is the news. Against within: with a future interval, in an hour means when the hour is up and within an hour means before it is; with a boundary, within the city limits is strictly inside a perimeter while in the city merely says where. Within is the precise, legalistic word, never reduces to a schwa, and has none of in's other senses — no within cash, no within Spanish, no within love. Against during: both locate an event inside a period, but during insists on the span while in merely names the container. Against inside: inside is the emphatic form that insists on the boundary and contrasts with an outside (inside the box, inside the city limits, inside an hour) while in is the neutral default — He's in the house is where he is, He's inside the house answers someone who thought he was in the yard. Against for in duration: after a negative or a superlative American English reaches for in where British English keeps for — I haven't seen him in years, the best game in a decade — and both varieties still allow for. Against the adverb particle in: the preposition always has an object (Come in the house), the particle never does (Come in).
entries.meaning: The preposition of the container. Its object is a bounded space you are inside — physically, geographically, temporally or metaphorically — and every sense projects that one image onto a different kind of boundary: a room, a country, a month, a language, a profession, a mood. It runs neck and neck with on for the most polysemous of the three and carries the most fixed collocations of any preposition in the language. Senses: 1. Enclosure (in the drawer, in the car). 2. An area or region — cities, states, countries, large spaces (in Cleveland, in the mountains). 3. Inside a text, image or performance (in chapter four, in the photo). 4. Months, seasons, years and long stretches of time, plus the general parts of the day — in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening, but not at night. 5. Time until something happens, and time taken to finish (the bus leaves in twenty minutes; read it in one sitting). 6. Elapsed time after a negative or a superlative — the distinctively American in for for (I haven't seen him in years, the coldest week in a decade), where British English keeps for. 7. Membership and participation (in the Navy, in a band). 8. A state, condition or set of circumstances (in love, in trouble, in debt, in a hurry, in ruins). 9. Ambient conditions — weather, light and temperature treated as a medium you stand inside (in the rain, in the snow, in the dark, in the sun, in the cold, in the fog). 10. Manner (in silence, in haste, in detail). 11. Medium, material or form — languages, substances, currencies, formats (in Spanish, in cash, in ink). 12. Clothing (the man in the gray coat). 13. Proportion and ratio (one in five). 14. A field or line of work (a degree in microbiology, in insurance). 15. The respect in which something is true (twelve feet in width, rich in iron, an increase in applications). 16. Arrangement (in twos, in half). 17. In + -ing, meaning in the very act of, formal and close to by or when (In signing the waiver, you give up the right to sue). 18. The domain of a superlative or a ranking, where many languages would use of (the oldest bar in Cincinnati, the only sophomore in the program). 19. Fixed adverbial and discourse phrases (in fact, in general, in short, in particular, in addition, in other words, in any case, in effect, in the meantime, in my opinion, in person). Stranding: in strands freely (the town I grew up in, This bed has been slept in) and pied-pipes formally (the town in which I grew up). Object test against the particle: the preposition has an object, the adverb does not — Come in (adverb) versus Come in the house (preposition), Fill it in versus Fill it in the box. Keep it apart also from the informal adjective (the in crowd), the noun (an in with the county) and the conjunction in that.
examples: The scissors are in the top drawer.
She waited in the car with the engine running.
They lived in Cleveland for six years.
There's still snow in the mountains.
It's explained in chapter four.
That's her in the second row of the photo.
The lease is up in August.
He started teaching in the nineties.
The bus leaves in twenty minutes.
She read the whole thing in one sitting.
We haven't had a summer like this in twenty years.
That's the first straight answer I've gotten out of him in months.
Both her sons are in the Navy.
He plays bass in a cover band.
They're in trouble with the county over the fence.
The whole building was in ruins by the time we got there.
They stood in the rain for two hours waiting for the gates to open.
Don't read in the dark.
The kids filed out in silence.
He said it in a way that ended the conversation.
The contract was drafted in Spanish.
He pays in cash and keeps every receipt.
The man in the gray coat never sat down.
She showed up in jeans and a blazer.
One in five households lost power.
The odds are about one in a thousand.
She has a degree in microbiology.
He's been in insurance his whole career.
The room is about twelve feet in width.
There's been a sharp increase in applications.
Line up in twos, please.
Cut the sandwich in half.
In signing the waiver, you give up the right to sue.
In trying to fix the leak, he cracked the pipe.
It's the oldest bar in Cincinnati.
She was the only sophomore in the entire program to place.
In fact, the second estimate was lower than the first.
She delivered the paperwork in person rather than mailing it.

entries.complement: noun phrase; pronoun in the objective case (on it, on them); gerund (insist on paying, on arriving); wh-clause (it depends on what she says, a guide on how to file). Never a bare infinitive (insist on to pay) and never a finite that-clause — depends on that he comes is impossible. Use whether (depends on whether he comes) or insert a noun: on the grounds that, on the assumption that, on the condition that.
entries.pattern: on [noun phrase] · on [verb-ing] · [verb] on [noun phrase] · [noun] on [noun phrase] (a tax on imports, a book on ethics) · stranded: What are you working on? — the shelf it was on · pied-piped (formal): the assumption on which the whole plan rests
entries.contrast: The surface member of the in / on / at system. Against in: surface versus enclosure — on the bus, the train, the plane (you can stand up in it) but in the car, the cab, a canoe (you sit down inside it). Against at: on the corner is a building located at an intersection, at the corner is the meeting point itself. Against onto: position versus the act of crossing onto a surface — The cat was on the roof is not The cat jumped onto the roof — though American English uses plain on freely with motion verbs (get on the bus). Against the two-word on to: keep the words apart whenever on belongs to the verb (hold on to the railing, move on to the next item, log on to the portal) and write one word only where to a position on top of fits (climb onto the railing). Against upon: upon is the formal, ceremonial and literary twin (once upon a time, upon arrival) and adds register but no meaning. Against about: a book on Roman history is systematic and expert, a book about Roman history is looser. Against over with the weekend and holidays: on the weekend names the block as a dated unit, over the weekend spreads an event across it, and only over works with a stretch you pass through (over Thanksgiving, over the summer). Against in for media the split is idiomatic rather than logical: a text is a container (in the paper, in the report) but a broadcast or network is a surface (on TV, on the radio), so the same story is in the Times and on Channel 4. Against the adverb particle on: the preposition has an object (Put your coat on the chair), the particle does not (Put your coat on).
entries.meaning: The preposition of the surface and the line. Its object supports something, is traced along, or is the medium something travels over — and from that come contact, routes, floors, calendars, broadcasts, platforms, and the large American set of on the team, on the board, on strike, on vacation. Senses: 1. Contact with a surface (on the counter, on the screen). 2. A line, edge, border or route — streets, rivers, coasts, boundaries, paths (on Lake Erie, on the way back). 3. A floor, a page, a list, a position in a layout (on the third floor, on page 212). 4. Aboard — anything you can stand up in or sit astride, plus on foot (on the train, on a bicycle). 5. A day or a date, including a day plus a part of the day, and in American English on the weekend (on March 3rd, on Thursdays). 6. At the moment of, formal, with a noun or gerund (on arrival, on hearing the verdict). 7. Topic — what a book, talk or comment is about (a textbook on soil chemistry, comment on the report). 8. Medium or device — broadcast, wire or instrument (on the news, on the phone). 9. Networks, platforms and apps, the modern extension of sense 8 and now one of the highest-frequency uses of the word (on the internet, on Instagram, on Zoom, on Slack, on the app); the platform is a surface you appear on, while a document stays a container (in the spreadsheet, in the thread). 10. Membership of a body you are picked or appointed to, distinctively American (on the school board, on the team). 11. Basis, dependence or fuel (rests on one email, runs on propane). 12. A state, process or activity under way (on strike, on sale, on fire, on duty, on call, on leave, on hold, on the mend). 13. A trip, an errand or an assignment — a journey or posting treated as a road you are out on (on vacation, on the road, on tour, on business, on assignment, on patrol, on a break). 14. Medication and regimens (on antibiotics, on a diet). 15. Paying for it (dinner's on me, on the house). 16. Directed at and often against — taxes, attacks, restrictions, betrayals (a tax on rentals, hard on yourself). 17. The person inconvenienced — the pronoun names whoever suffers the event, not the target (My laptop quit on me; She hung up on him). 18. Carried on one's person (Do you have a pen on you?). 19. Fixed adverbial and discourse phrases (on purpose, on average, on the whole, on the other hand, on the contrary, on balance, on time, on hand, on end, on second thought). Stranding: on strands freely (What are you working on?, the shelf it was on) and pied-pipes formally (the assumption on which the plan rests). Object test against the particle: the preposition has an object, the particle does not — Put your coat on (particle) versus Put your coat on the chair (preposition); Drive on, later on, from then on, and so on are all objectless. Note also the two-word on to (Hold on to the railing) against the one-word onto (Climb onto the railing).
examples: Your keys are on the counter.
There's a smudge on the screen.
Their place is on Lake Erie.
We stopped for gas on the way back.
Radiology is on the third floor.
The footnote is on page 212.
I left my umbrella on the train.
She crossed the whole state on a bicycle.
The closing is on March 3rd.
He works late on Thursdays.
On arrival, please check in at the front desk.
On hearing the verdict, half the room stood up.
She wrote the standard textbook on soil chemistry.
The senator refused to comment on the report.
It was on the news all morning.
I'll be on the phone for another minute.
Half the class only knows her on Instagram.
We'll do the walkthrough on Zoom at four.
She's on the school board now.
Both twins made it on the team.
The whole argument rests on one email.
The generator runs on propane.
The nurses have been on strike for two weeks.
Everything in the store is on sale through Sunday.
He's on the road three weeks out of every month.
She's on assignment in Phoenix until the end of the quarter.
He's on antibiotics for another five days.
She's been on a low-sodium diet since March.
Dinner's on me tonight.
The first round is on the house.
The council imposed a new tax on short-term rentals.
Don't be too hard on yourself.
My laptop quit on me halfway through the exam.
She hung up on him twice.
Do you have a pen on you?
I never carry cash on me anymore.
He did it on purpose, and everyone knew it.
On the whole, the first draft held up better than we expected.

entries.complement: noun phrase; pronoun in the objective case (into it, into them); gerund (talked her into staying, got into arguing about money, ran into trouble finding parking); wh-clause, chiefly in the inquiry sense (an investigation into what went wrong, I'll look into how that happened, no insight into why she left). Never a bare infinitive — talked her into to stay is impossible — and never a finite that-clause: an inquiry into that the money vanished has to become an inquiry into the fact that the money vanished. Into has no adverb use at all; like at, it always has an object, even a stranded one.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] into [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] into [noun phrase] · into [verb-ing] · into [wh-clause] · stranded: the room she walked into — What have you gotten yourself into? · pied-piped (formal): the state into which the house had fallen
entries.contrast: Against in: position versus crossing — He was in the pool is not He jumped into the pool — though American English lets plain in do the motion job after everyday verbs (jump in the pool, throw it in the trash). Against the two-word in to: keep them apart whenever in belongs to the verb — turned himself in to the police (he surrendered) is not turned himself into the police (he became them); likewise came in to talk, dropped in to say hi, tuned in to the broadcast. Against onto: interior versus surface, exactly as with in and on — fell into the pool but fell onto the deck. Against to: to names a destination reached, into insists a boundary was crossed — drove to the garage stops at it, drove into the garage ends up inside. The two-word sequence has its own entry as in to.
entries.meaning: The general preposition of entry: motion from outside to inside, with the boundary crossed. Every other sense is that image applied to something that is not a room — a wall you hit, a state you turn into, an action you break into, a night you work deep into, a subject you look inside. Senses: 1. Motion to a position inside (walked into the kitchen, pour it into the pan). 2. Motion ending in collision or forced contact (backed into a mailbox). 3. Change of state, form or language, after turn, change, translate, convert, break, grow, make (turned into a shouting match, translate into Spanish). 4. Entry into an action or an outburst — the start of an activity treated as a space you break into (break into a run, burst into tears, launch into a speech, go into detail, get into an argument); the action begins abruptly, which is why broke into a run is not began to run. 5. Penetration into a period or a distance (rehearsing into the early morning, three weeks into the semester). 6. Inquiry or investigation (an investigation into the missing funds, look into what happened). 7. Persuasion or pressure, always with a gerund (talked her into running, pushed him into selling). 8. Enthusiasm for, informal and only predicative (into woodworking, not into horror movies). 9. Chance encounter, with run and bump (ran into my old landlord). 10. Division in arithmetic (four into twenty). Stranding: into strands normally (the mess we got into, What did she change into?) and pied-pipes stiffly. Because it has no particle twin, a stranded into is always the preposition — but watch the reverse error of splitting it: He got into trouble, never He got in to trouble.
examples: She walked into the kitchen without knocking.
Pour the batter into the pan and level it off.
He backed into a mailbox on the first try.
The truck slid into the guardrail.
The argument turned into a shouting match.
Translate the whole section into Spanish by Friday.
He broke into a run before the light changed.
She burst into tears in the middle of the toast.
They kept rehearsing into the early morning.
We were three weeks into the semester before anyone noticed.
The board opened an investigation into the missing funds.
I'll look into what happened with your order.
They talked her into running for the seat.
Nobody pushed him into selling the house.
He's been into woodworking since he retired.
She's not into horror movies at all.
I ran into my old landlord at the hardware store.
We bumped into each other outside the courthouse.
Four into twenty goes five times.
Divide the class into groups of three.

entries.complement: noun phrase; pronoun in the objective case (onto it, onto them); wh-clause in the informal aware-of sense only (they're onto what he's been doing, she's onto how the scheme works) — everywhere else a clause is impossible. Gerunds are marginal at best — onto winning is not idiomatic, and where a gerund is wanted writers use the two-word on to instead (moved on to fixing the roof); this is the one clear complement difference between onto and into, which takes gerunds readily. Never a bare infinitive and never a finite that-clause: onto that he was lying is impossible, and the repair is onto the fact that he was lying. Onto has no adverb use: it always has an object.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] onto [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] onto [noun phrase] · stranded: the ledge he climbed onto — the flash drive I copied it onto
entries.contrast: Against on: position versus crossing — The cat was on the roof is not The cat jumped onto the roof. Against the two-word on to, which is the error American writers actually make: if to a position on top of fits, write one word; if on belongs to the verb (hold on, move on, pass on, hang on, log on, sign on, catch on, go on), keep two — hold on to the rail (gripped it) versus climbed onto the rail (got up on it), log on to the server, not log onto the server. The one genuine gray area is be on to someone (have figured out what they are up to), written both ways in edited American prose with onto now slightly commoner. Against into: surface versus interior — loaded it onto the truck (on the bed) but loaded it into the truck (in the cab).
entries.meaning: The surface counterpart of into: motion that ends with the moving thing resting on top of something. The extensions treat a drive, a bill, or a person as a surface you land on. Senses: 1. Motion to a position on a surface (stepped onto the platform, leapt onto the counter). 2. Transfer onto a surface or a medium (copy the files onto a flash drive, load the boxes onto the truck). 3. Emergence or outlook onto an open space, with open, look, give, back (the door opens onto the alley, looks onto the parking lot). 4. Adding to an existing base — charges, additions, extensions (tacked a resort fee onto the bill, bolted a sunroom onto the house). 5. Shifting a burden or a feeling onto a person, who becomes the surface the load lands on (offload it onto, dump it onto, pin the blame onto, project his anxiety onto) — the psychological cousin of sense 2 and one of the few places where onto clearly beats plain on. 6. Aware of, having caught on to, informal (they've been onto you for weeks, she's onto something). Stranding: onto strands but reluctantly (the shelf I put it onto — most speakers prefer the shelf I put it on), and it pied-pipes almost never. Where the surface is already established, plain on is the more natural American choice: put it on the shelf beats put it onto the shelf.
examples: She stepped onto the platform just as the doors closed.
The cat leapt onto the counter the second we left.
Copy the files onto a flash drive before you wipe the laptop.
Load the boxes onto the truck first.
The kitchen door opens onto the alley.
Their balcony looks onto the parking lot.
The hotel tacked a resort fee onto the bill.
They bolted a sunroom onto the back of the house.
He projects every bad mood onto whoever's nearest.
They dumped the whole reconciliation onto the new hire.
Don't bother lying — they've been onto you for weeks.
I think she's onto something with that theory.

entries.ipa: /əˈpɑn/ ~ /əˈpɔn/, first syllable always a schwa and never stressed
entries.register: formal, literary, or fixed-phrase; in plain modern American prose on is the default
entries.complement: noun phrase; pronoun in the objective case (upon it, upon them); gerund (upon signing the contract, upon arriving at the site) — the one place upon genuinely beats on in modern writing; wh-clause, exactly as with on (it depends upon what the auditor finds, acted upon what he had been told, seized upon whichever number helped). Never a bare infinitive (upon to sign) and never a finite that-clause: upon that he arrived is impossible, and the clause version is when he arrived or once he had arrived. Upon has no adverb use; the objectless on in later on can never be later upon.
entries.pattern: [verb] upon [noun phrase] · Upon [noun phrase / verb-ing], [main clause] · [noun] upon [the same noun] (row upon row) · stranded only marginally: the fate they had stumbled upon
entries.contrast: Against on: the same meaning at a higher register. Upon is longer, heavier and more formal, and reaching for it to sound elegant is the classic overcorrection — sit upon the couch is simply worse than sit on the couch. Reserve it for the four places it earns its keep: after certain verbs (depend upon, call upon, seize upon, act upon), in the temporal upon + gerund, in the doubling pattern (row upon row), and in frozen phrases (once upon a time). Against onto: in its motion sense upon is a near-synonym of onto with a sudden or forceful edge — armies descend upon a town, not onto it.
entries.meaning: The elevated twin of on, useful in exactly the places where its extra weight buys something. Its most genuinely modern job is temporal: upon arrival and upon signing compress a whole clause into two words, which is why contracts, instructions and signage are full of it. Senses: 1. On a surface, formal or literary (snow lay upon the fields, the inscription upon the stone). 2. Motion onto, often sudden or forceful (winter descended upon the valley, the dogs fell upon the scraps). 3. Immediately after, with a noun or a gerund (upon arrival, upon signing). 4. Discourse frames of reconsideration, where upon is standard and plain on sounds wrong (upon reflection, upon closer inspection, upon consideration, upon due deliberation) — sports broadcasting is the exception that keeps on further review. 5. Chance encounter, with come, happen, stumble (happened upon the letter, stumbled upon the wreck). 6. Doubling for quantity — the same noun repeated with no article, singular in mile upon mile and plural in thousands upon thousands. 7. Fixed verb and noun collocations (depend upon, call upon, seize upon, act upon, insist upon, look upon, impose upon, prevail upon) — every one of which also works with on, and most of which are commoner with it. Stranding: upon strands only reluctantly (the discovery they had stumbled upon); most writers either pied-pipe (the discovery upon which the case rests) or drop to on.
examples: A heavy snow lay upon the fields.
The inscription upon the stone had worn away.
Winter descended upon the valley all at once.
The dogs fell upon the scraps before anyone could stop them.
Upon arrival, report to the front desk.
Upon signing, you'll receive a copy of the agreement.
Upon reflection, I'd rather not put my name on it.
Upon closer inspection, the signature turned out to be stamped.
I happened upon the letter while cleaning out the attic.
They stumbled upon the wreck by accident.
Mile upon mile of the same brown grass.
Thousands upon thousands of people showed up.
The whole plan depends upon the county approving the variance.
She was called upon to testify twice.
